stem: A cluster administrator configures a Gateway with a TCPRoute in an environment where Cilium host network mode is enabled. How does the traffic for this TCPRoute behave compared to standard Gateway listener traffic?

stem: A cluster administrator wants to mitigate the risk of unencrypted egress traffic to not-yet-discovered remote endpoints by ensuring that traffic exiting a node to a specific set of IP addresses is always encrypted. Which configuration should they apply?

options.text: Set encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and define the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr.
Enable encryption.strictMode.ingress.enabled to drop any cluster-internal ingress traffic that did not arrive via the WireGuard tunnel.
Configure a network policy that allows egress traffic to reserved:world identities to ensure all external traffic is routed through the tunnel.
Set encryption.strictMode.egress.allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false to block all traffic associated with node identities.

explanation: The excerpt identifies setting encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled to true and the expected pod CIDR as encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr as a way to mitigate the issue by enforcing that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

optionRationale.b: Strict mode ingress protects local endpoints from unencrypted ingress traffic, not egress traffic from the node to remote endpoints.
optionRationale.c: Allowing traffic to reserved:world is identified as a condition that makes the unencrypted leak possible, not a mitigation. The mitigation is to restrict this or use strict mode.
optionRationale.d: Setting allowRemoteNodeIdentities to false is not the primary mitigation described for the general pod CIDR; it is a specific setting related to node identities when not using direct routing mode.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: Another way to mitigate this issue is to set ``encryption.strictMode.egress.enabled`` to ``true`` and the expected pod CIDR as ``encryption.strictMode.egress.cidr``. This encryption strict mode egress enforces that traffic exiting a node to the set CIDR is always encrypted.

stem: An engineer is configuring encryption strict mode egress for a cluster that uses IPv6 for pod communication. What limitation must they be aware of regarding the protection of this traffic?

options.text: IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.
IPv6 traffic requires the use of direct routing mode to be protected by strict mode egress.
IPv6 traffic is protected only if the node CIDR and pod CIDR do not overlap.
IPv6 traffic is automatically encrypted using the node identity key regardless of the strict mode configuration.

explanation: The excerpt explicitly lists as a limitation that the pod CIDR and therefore the encryption strict mode egress CIDR must be IPv4, and that IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that direct routing mode is required to disable dynamic lookups, but it does not state that it enables IPv6 protection; in fact, it states IPv6 is not protected.
optionRationale.c: The non-overlapping CIDR requirement is related to disabling dynamic lookups and node identities, not specifically to enabling IPv6 protection.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that IPv6 traffic can be leaked, implying it is not automatically protected.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: The pod CIDR and therefore the encryption strict mode egress CIDR must be IPv4. IPv6 traffic is not protected by the strict mode and can be leaked.

stem: A security audit reveals that an attacker could inject unencrypted pod traffic through a network interface on a node that Cilium does not manage. Which aspect of encryption strict mode ingress does this scenario highlight?

options.text: Enforcement relies on Cilium's BPF programs being attached to all pod-routable network interfaces.
Node-to-node encryption for WireGuard is not protected by strict mode ingress.
Strict mode ingress is not supported when chaining Cilium on top of other CNI plugins.
The WireGuard tunnel must be established before any ingress traffic is processed.

explanation: The excerpt states that enforcement relies on Cilium's BPF programs being attached to all pod-routable network interfaces, and that if a node has additional interfaces that Cilium does not manage, an attacker could inject unencrypted pod traffic through those interfaces.

optionRationale.b: While true that node-to-node encryption is not protected, the specific scenario of injecting traffic through an unmanaged interface is explained by the reliance on BPF program attachment to all relevant interfaces.
optionRationale.c: This is a separate limitation regarding CNI chaining, not the specific mechanism of interface-based enforcement described in the scenario.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt does not state that the tunnel must be established before processing; it states that traffic not arriving through the tunnel is dropped.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: Enforcement relies on Cilium's BPF programs being attached to all pod-routable network interfaces. If the node has additional interfaces that Cilium does not manage (and therefore has no BPF program attached to), an attacker could inject unencrypted pod traffic through those interfaces, bypassing strict mode ingress.

stem: Which of the following statements accurately describes the support status of encryption strict mode ingress with different encryption technologies?

options.text: It is supported with both tunnel and native routing modes, and requires WireGuard encryption.
It is supported with IPsec encryption but not with WireGuard.
It is only supported in tunnel mode and requires IPsec encryption.
It is supported with both WireGuard and IPsec, provided direct routing mode is used.

explanation: The excerpt states that strict mode ingress is supported with both tunnel and native routing modes, and requires WireGuard encryption (it is not supported with IPsec).

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly states it is not supported with IPsec.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states it is supported with native routing modes as well, and requires WireGuard, not IPsec.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states it is not supported with IPsec.

citations.title: Egress traffic to not yet discovered remote endpoints may be unencrypted
citations.quote: Strict mode ingress is supported with both tunnel and native routing modes, and requires WireGuard encryption (it is not supported with IPsec).

stem: An engineer configures a Hubble metric with `flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`. During a specific flow, the DNS name for the destination is not known. What value will be used for the `destination` label in the metric?

options.text: The IP address of the destination
An empty string
The Kubernetes namespace of the destination
The reserved identity label

explanation: The excerpt states that when multiple contexts are specified, the first non-empty value is added to the metric as a label. It explicitly gives the example that if no DNS name is known, it will fall back and use the IP address of the target instead.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt states that the first non-empty value is used, implying a fallback occurs rather than an empty label being forced if a subsequent option is available.
optionRationale.c: The namespace is not part of the specified `dns|ip` chain, so it is not considered for the fallback.
optionRationale.d: The reserved identity is not part of the specified `dns|ip` chain, so it is not considered for the fallback.

citations.title: Context Options
citations.quote: For example, a metric configuration of ``flow:destinationContext=dns|ip`` will first try to use the DNS name of the target for the label. If no DNS name is known for the target, it will fall back and use the IP address of the target instead.

stem: A network engineer wants to configure Hubble metrics to include the Kubernetes namespace name for the source of the traffic. Which context option value should be used in the `sourceContext` configuration?

options.text: namespace
pod
identity
workload

explanation: The table of option values lists `namespace` with the description 'Kubernetes namespace name'. The `pod` option includes both name and namespace, `identity` includes all security labels, and `workload` includes the workload name and namespace.

optionRationale.b: The `pod` option provides the pod name and namespace in the form of `namespace/pod`, which is more specific than just the namespace name.
optionRationale.c: The `identity` option provides all Cilium security identity labels, not just the namespace.
optionRationale.d: The `workload` option provides the workload name and namespace, not just the namespace.

stem: An operator wants Cilium to determine the upper capacity limits of several large BPF maps at agent startup from a proportion of the node's total system memory, rather than setting each map's capacity individually. Which cilium-agent option should the operator use?

options.text: --bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio
--bpf-ct-global-tcp-max
--bpf-lb-map-max
--bpf-nat-global-max

explanation: The excerpt states that using the --bpf-map-dynamic-size-ratio flag, the upper capacity limits of several large BPF maps are determined at agent startup based on the given ratio of the total system memory. The other listed flags are command-line options for setting a given capacity, not for deriving several large map limits from a memory ratio.

optionRationale.b: --bpf-ct-global-tcp-max is listed as a command-line option for setting a given capacity, not for sizing several large BPF maps from a ratio of total system memory.
optionRationale.c: --bpf-lb-map-max is listed as a command-line option for setting a given capacity, not for sizing several large BPF maps from a ratio of total system memory.
optionRationale.d: --bpf-nat-global-max is listed as a command-line option for setting a given capacity, not for sizing several large BPF maps from a ratio of total system memory.

stem: You are validating a Hubble installation and run `kubectl get configmap -n kube-system cilium-config -oyaml | grep hubble-disable-tls`. The output shows `hubble-disable-tls: "false"`. What does this tell you before you proceed with the remaining validation steps?

options.text: TLS has been configured correctly for Hubble, because the option that would disable it is set to false.
TLS is currently disabled for Hubble and must be switched on before any further validation can take place.
The value is a placeholder written by the Hubble CLI pod, which has not yet been created in the cluster.
Hubble Relay is running, but the Hubble server certificate has expired and must be renewed.

explanation: The excerpt instructs you to verify the configuration before beginning, and states that you should see the `hubble-disable-tls` configuration option set to `false`. A value of `false` therefore means TLS is not being disabled, that is, it has been configured correctly, and you can continue with the validation procedure.

optionRationale.b: This inverts the meaning of the flag: `false` means TLS is not disabled, so it is not a signal that TLS must be switched on.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt presents the check as the first step, performed before the Hubble CLI pod is created, and attaches no placeholder meaning to the value.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing here about certificate expiry; expiry is not what this configuration option reports.

citations.title: Validating the Installation
citations.quote: You should see that the ``hubble-disable-tls`` configuration option is set to ``false``.

stem: You have created the Hubble CLI pod in `kube-system` and run `hubble watch peers --server unix:///var/run/cilium/hubble.sock`. Peers are listed, but no `TLS.ServerName` appears beside them. What does this indicate?

options.text: TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server, and the following validation steps will not work.
TLS is enabled, but the server name is only shown for peers that are reached through Hubble Relay rather than the local socket.
The Hubble CLI pod is missing the relay client certificate, so the server name cannot be resolved.
The peers are healthy; the server name is only displayed when `--tls-server-name` is passed to `hubble watch peers`.

explanation: The excerpt warns explicitly that if the `TLS.ServerName` is missing from the output, TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server and the following steps will not work, and it directs you back to the previous sections to enable TLS. The absence of the field is therefore a signal about the server's TLS configuration, not about the CLI pod's credentials.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt draws no distinction between peers reached over the socket and peers reached through the relay; the missing field simply means TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server.
optionRationale.c: The command is run against the local socket, and the excerpt attributes a missing server name to TLS not being enabled on the server, not to a missing client certificate.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt gives no such flag for `hubble watch peers`; the server name appears in the peer listing itself when TLS is enabled.

citations.title: Validating the Installation
citations.quote: If the ``TLS.ServerName`` is missing from your output then TLS is not enabled for the Hubble server and the following steps will not work.

stem: From the Hubble CLI pod you query the first peer with `hubble observe --server tls://${IP?}:4244 --tls-server-name ${SERVERNAME?} --tls-ca-cert-files /var/lib/hubble-relay/tls/hubble-server-ca.crt`, deliberately omitting the client certificate and key. What happens, and why?

options.text: The command fails with exit code 1 and a TLS error stating that a certificate is required, because the server expects clients to present a certificate.
The command succeeds, because supplying the CA certificate file is sufficient to authenticate the client to the server.
The command fails with `error reading server preface: EOF`, because the server only accepts plaintext connections on that port.
The command succeeds but returns only flows involving the host endpoint, since unauthenticated clients see a restricted view.

explanation: The excerpt contrasts two attempts: one using the Hubble Relay client certificate, which confirms that the server accepts clients presenting the correct certificate, and one made without any client certificate, which fails with a TLS error reporting that a certificate is required and terminates with exit code 1. The CA file alone verifies the server; it does not authenticate the client.

optionRationale.b: The CA certificate file is used to verify the server's certificate; the excerpt shows the connection still failing when no client certificate is supplied.
optionRationale.c: The `EOF` error belongs to the separate attempt made without TLS at all, not to a TLS connection that lacks a client certificate.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the command terminating with exit code 1 rather than returning a restricted set of flows.

citations.title: Validating the Installation
citations.quote: failed to connect to '172.18.0.2:4244': context deadline exceeded: connection error: desc = "error reading server preface: remote error: tls: certificate requiredd"

stem: A cluster runs with `multi-pool` as its IPAM mode. Its `default` CiliumPodIPPool lists the CIDR `10.10.0.0/16`, and nginx pods are running on both `kind-worker` and `kind-control-plane`. An engineer applies an updated `default` pool whose only CIDR is now `10.20.0.0/16`, then restarts the Cilium operator. What does the operator do about the old CIDRs?

options.text: It reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool.
It rejects the update and keeps the pool at `10.10.0.0/16` until every pod on the cluster has been restarted.
It immediately re-addresses every running pod from `10.20.0.0/16` without any further action being taken.
It deletes the `CiliumPodIPPool` and waits for `autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` to recreate it from the Helm values.

explanation: After the pool is updated and the Cilium operator restarted, the operator reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by a node but removed from the pool — in the worked example, `10.10.0.0/24` on `kind-control-plane` and `10.10.1.0/24` on `kind-worker`. The update is accepted rather than rejected, and running pods are not re-addressed automatically: the restriction exists precisely to prevent pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes. Moving workloads onto the new CIDR requires the node-group migration steps that follow.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the updated pool being applied successfully and the operator merely logging warnings; nothing in it describes the update being rejected.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the restriction prevents pods from receiving IPs from a new range while some pods still use the old IP pool on the same nodes, so re-addressing is not automatic — pods only pick up the new range once they are evicted and rescheduled.
optionRationale.d: Deleting the existing `CiliumPodIPPools` belongs to the separate `autoCreateCiliumPodIPPools` alternative, not to what the operator does when a pool is updated in place.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: Note how the Cilium operator reports a warning for each CIDR block still in use by node but removed from the pool:

stem: An engineer has an existing `CiliumPodIPPool` named `default` that pods on the cluster are already using, and wants to modify that resource in place. Which modification does the excerpt say is possible?

options.text: Extending the pool by adding a new IPv6 CIDR alongside the existing ones.
Replacing an in-use IPv4 CIDR with a different range in a single apply.
Removing one of several CIDRs from the pool while keeping the others.
Shrinking an in-use CIDR to a smaller range so that fewer addresses are handed out.

explanation: Updates to an existing `CiliumPodIPPools` are subject to limitations: the pool can be extended by adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but CIDRs already in use cannot be deleted or updated. Replacing, removing or shrinking an in-use CIDR therefore falls on the forbidden side of that line. The excerpt adds that if you have no other choice than updating in-use CIDRs, the node-group migration procedure should be used as a reference instead.

optionRationale.b: Replacing an in-use CIDR is an update to a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt says is not possible; the worked example only gets there by splitting the cluster into two node groups and migrating workloads.
optionRationale.c: Removing a CIDR is a deletion of a CIDR already in use, which the excerpt explicitly rules out.
optionRationale.d: Shrinking an in-use CIDR is still an update to a CIDR already in use, so it is not among the permitted changes.

citations.title: Updating existing CiliumPodIPPools
citations.quote: It is possible to extend the pool adding new IPv4 or IPv6 CIDRs, but it is not possible to delete or update the CIDRs already in use.

stem: You run two clusters joined by Cluster Mesh. A global Service named rebel-base already exists, and in cluster 1 you run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=local --overwrite`. You then curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1 while healthy backends exist in both clusters. What do you observe?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only, because the local backends are preferred while they remain healthy.
The replies come from pods in both clusters, because a global Service always balances across every cluster.
The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only, because the annotation pushes traffic away from the local cluster.
No replies arrive until the annotation is removed, because the local preference blocks remote endpoints permanently.

explanation: Setting the affinity annotation to local makes the Global Service prefer healthy backends in the local cluster. Remote endpoints are used only as a fallback, so a client in cluster 1 keeps being served by cluster 1 pods for as long as those backends are available and healthy.

optionRationale.b: This is the behaviour without any affinity preference; the local value deliberately overrides it while local backends are healthy.
optionRationale.c: That is the effect of the remote value, not the local value.
optionRationale.d: Remote endpoints are not blocked permanently; they are used if and only if all local backends are unavailable or unhealthy.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity

stem: Continuing with the same global Service, you now run `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity=remote --overwrite` in cluster 1 and curl rebel-base from a pod in cluster 1. What is the result?

options.text: The replies come from pods in cluster 2 only.
The replies come from pods in cluster 1 only.
The replies come from pods in both clusters as usual.
The request fails, because a cluster cannot prefer endpoints it does not host.

explanation: Switching the annotation to remote inverts the preference: the endpoints of the other cluster become the preferred destination, so a client in cluster 1 is served by cluster 2 pods.

optionRationale.b: That is what the local value produces, not the remote value.
optionRationale.c: That is the behaviour with no affinity preference, or when the client sits in the cluster that is not the preferred one.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows the request succeeding and being answered by cluster 2 pods.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: This time, the replies are coming from pods in ``cluster 2`` only.

stem: A global Service carries no `service.cilium.io/affinity` annotation at all. What preference does Cilium apply?

options.text: None — there is no preference, which is the default behaviour when the annotation does not exist.
Local — endpoints in the local cluster are preferred whenever they are available.
Remote — endpoints in remote clusters are preferred whenever they are available.
Global — the service is balanced strictly across all clusters with no local endpoints considered.

explanation: The annotation accepts none, local and remote. The value none is the default and means no preference, and it is also the behaviour applied when the annotation is absent altogether.

optionRationale.b: Local is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.c: Remote is an explicit value that must be set; it is not the default.
optionRationale.d: Global is not one of the listed values for this annotation; the global behaviour comes from the separate service.cilium.io/global annotation.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
# - none (default)
     #    no preference. Default behavior if this annotation does not exist

stem: Your platform uses MCS-API for multi-cluster services, and you want a global Service to prefer endpoints in the local cluster. Where do you specify the affinity setting in this setup?

options.text: Through the `exportedAnnotations` field of the ServiceExport.
Through an `importedAnnotations` field on the ServiceImport.
Through a command-line flag on the Cilium agent DaemonSet.
Through the `service.cilium.io/global` annotation on the Service itself.

explanation: When MCS-API is in use, the affinity annotation is not placed directly on the Service; it is specified through the ServiceExport's exportedAnnotations field.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names the ServiceExport and its exportedAnnotations field, not a field on the ServiceImport.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt describes an annotation-based mechanism, not an agent command-line flag.
optionRationale.d: service.cilium.io/global is the separate annotation that marks a Service as global; it does not carry the affinity preference.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote:
With :ref:`MCS-API
<gs_clustermesh_mcsapi>`, specify this annotation through the ServiceExport
``exportedAnnotations`` field.

stem: A global Service in cluster 1 has `service.cilium.io/affinity=remote` set. An operator runs `kubectl annotate service rebel-base service.cilium.io/affinity- --overwrite` in cluster 1, then curls the service from either cluster. What happens?

options.text: Replies come from pods in both clusters again, because the preference has been cleared.
Replies still come from cluster 2 only, because the preference is cached by the agent.
Replies come from cluster 1 only, because removing the annotation defaults to local.
The Service stops being global and only local endpoints remain reachable.

explanation: Removing the affinity annotation returns the Service to the no-preference default, so traffic is once again spread over the backends of both clusters.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt shows the behaviour changing immediately after the annotation is removed.
optionRationale.c: The default when the annotation does not exist is no preference, not local.
optionRationale.d: Only the affinity annotation is removed; the Service remains a global Service.

citations.title: Enabling Global Service Affinity
citations.quote: You will see replies from pods in both clusters again.

stem: An engineer writes a CiliumNetworkPolicy rule that selects a set of endpoints with endpointSelector but omits both the ingress and egress sections. What is the effect of this rule?

options.text: The rule has no effect.
The rule denies all ingress and egress traffic for the selected endpoints.
The rule allows all ingress and egress traffic for the selected endpoints.
The rule applies only at ingress, because an omitted egress section defaults to an empty allow list.

explanation: The excerpt states that either ingress, egress, or both can be provided, and that if both are omitted the rule has no effect. Selecting endpoints alone does not turn the rule into an allow rule or a deny rule.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not say that omitting both sections creates a deny rule; it says the rule has no effect.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not say that omitting both sections allows all traffic; it says the rule has no effect.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt treats ingress and egress symmetrically here: either can be provided, but if both are omitted the rule has no effect.

citations.title: Rule Basics
citations.quote: Either ingress, egress, or both can be provided. If both ingress and egress are omitted, the rule has no effect.

stem: An engineer wants to know which namespaces in the cluster have had network flows during the past hour, so that they can narrow down where to start troubleshooting. Which Observer service RPC endpoint should they call?

options.text: `GetNamespaces`
`GetNodes`
`ServerStatus`
`GetFlows`

explanation: `GetNamespaces` is the endpoint that reports namespaces which had network flows within the last one hour, which is exactly the time-bounded list the engineer needs. `GetNodes` reports per-Hubble-instance metrics and other information, `ServerStatus` summarises that same node information, and `GetFlows` streams flow events rather than listing namespaces.

optionRationale.b: ``GetNodes`` returns a list of metrics and other information related to each Hubble instance, not a list of namespaces with recent flows.
optionRationale.c: ``ServerStatus`` returns a summary of the information in ``GetNodes``, so it describes Hubble instances rather than namespaces.
optionRationale.d: ``GetFlows`` returns a stream of flow related events; it does not produce a list of namespaces active in the last hour.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: ``GetNamespaces`` returns a list of namespaces that had network flows within the last one hour.

stem: A caller issues a `GetFlows` request that supplies both an allow list and a deny list. A particular flow matches the allow list and also matches the deny list. What does the caller receive?

options.text: The flow is absent from the result, because the result contains only flows matched by the allow list that are not simultaneously matched by the deny list.
The flow is present, because a flow only needs to match one of the supplied filters to be included.
The flow is present, because the allow list always takes precedence over the deny list when both are supplied.
The flow is present twice, once for the allow list match and once for the deny list match.

explanation: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result contains all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list. A flow that matches both lists is therefore excluded. The rule that only one of multiple flow filters has to match applies to filters of the same kind, and it does not override the interaction between an allow list and a deny list.

optionRationale.b: The 'only one has to match' rule describes multiple flow filters of the same kind; it does not mean a flow matching both an allow and a deny list survives.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: flows matched by the allow list are removed when they are also simultaneously matched by the deny list.
optionRationale.d: Nothing in the excerpt describes duplicate delivery; the deny list removes flows from the allow list result rather than adding to it.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: When both allow and deny filters are specified, the result will contain all flows matched by the allow list that are not also simultaneously matched by the deny list.

stem: An engineer is reasoning about how many events a Hubble ring buffer can hold, having read that the internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1. Which statement describes the capacity from a user perspective?

options.text: The capacity is one less than a power of 2, because one slot is reserved for the writer.
The capacity is exactly a power of 2, with every slot available to readers.
The capacity is one more than a power of 2, because the writer slot is added on top of the mask.
The capacity is exactly the configured number of events, with no slot reserved for the writer.

explanation: The internal buffer length is a bit mask of ones + 1, and the internal buffer size is always a power of 2 with 1 slot reserved for the writer. From a user perspective this means the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

optionRationale.b: A power of 2 is the internal buffer size, but one slot is reserved for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is one less than that.
optionRationale.c: The reserved writer slot is taken out of the power-of-2 size rather than added to it, so the capacity is one less, not one more.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt explicitly reserves one slot for the writer, so the user-visible capacity is not the full configured figure.

citations.title: The Observer service
citations.quote: In effect, from a user perspective, the ring buffer capacity is one less than a power of 2.

stem: An engineer wants to narrow down Cilium datapath debug events by supplying allow and deny filters to the `GetDebugEvents` RPC endpoint, in the same way they do for `GetFlows`. What is the outcome?

options.text: The filters have no effect, because `GetDebugEvents` does not implement filtering capabilities.
The filters are applied exactly as they are for `GetFlows`, including the allow-list and deny-list interaction.
Only deny lists are honoured; allow lists are silently ignored on this endpoint.
The filters are applied, but only to events that also appear in `GetAgentEvents`.

explanation: `GetAgentEvents` and `GetDebugEvents` are similar to `GetFlows` except that they do not implement filtering capabilities. Supplying allow and deny lists to `GetDebugEvents` therefore does not narrow the returned debug events.

optionRationale.b: The filtering behaviour described for ``GetFlows`` is precisely what these two endpoints lack.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt makes no such distinction between allow and deny lists here; neither form of filtering is implemented.

stem: A Hubble instance has been running for a long time and its ring buffer has become full, while a ring reader in follow mode continues to read events as they are written. What happens to the events already stored in the buffer?

options.text: They are overridden by newer events, because events are continuously consumed and older ones are overridden once the ring buffer is full.
They are retained indefinitely and new events are dropped until the reader has drained the buffer.
They are written out to disk so that the in-memory buffer can be reused.
They are preserved because the ring buffer grows dynamically to accommodate new events.

explanation: Hubble stores monitoring events in a user-space ring buffer that holds a configurable amount of events in memory. Events are continuously consumed, overriding older ones once the ring buffer is full, so the oldest stored events are lost as new ones arrive.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes older events being overridden, not new events being dropped while the reader catches up.
optionRationale.c: The buffer is described as storing events in memory; no spilling of events to disk is mentioned.
optionRationale.d: The buffer stores a configurable amount of events and overrides older ones when full; it is not described as growing dynamically.

It is required, because externalTrafficPolicy: Cluster always masquerades the source IP, so the backend Pod can never see it.
It is unnecessary, but only if the healthCheckNodePort is manually configured so that every node passes the health check.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium 1.16 with Hubble metrics already enabled. They want the Hubble metrics API to be served over TLS, but they do not want Prometheus to have to present a client certificate. Which single Helm option should they add to their install or upgrade command?

options.text: --set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.enabled=true
--set hubble.metrics.tls.server.mtls.name=hubble-metrics-ca
--set hubble.tls.enabled=true

explanation: The excerpt states that TLS on the Hubble metrics API is switched on with the Helm flag --set hubble.metrics.tls.enabled=true. The mTLS flags are only needed when client authentication is also wanted, and the excerpt gives no flag of the form hubble.tls.enabled.

optionRationale.b: This flag enables mTLS authentication on the metrics API, which would require clients to present certificates — more than the team asked for.
optionRationale.c: This flag only names the ConfigMap holding the CA certificate; it is used alongside the mTLS flags and does not on its own turn on TLS.
optionRationale.d: No such flag appears in the excerpt; the documented flag is scoped under hubble.metrics.tls.

stem: A platform team runs a shared cluster. They want the developers of one application team to be able to create Route objects in that team's own namespace, while ensuring those developers cannot modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in any other namespace. Which aspect of the Gateway API's design is intended to make this kind of arrangement possible?

options.text: The Ingress API is deconstructed into several Gateway API objects, each aligned to a role-based persona, so that each persona gains only the specific access and privileges its responsibilities require.
Gateway API resources carry annotations that record which team owns them, and the implementation uses those annotations to restrict who may edit the resource.
The Gateway API promotes features to API conformance, which automatically grants each namespace owner write access to the Gateway configuration.
The Gateway API provides a centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination and traffic splitting, and this centralisation removes the need for per-namespace permissions.

explanation: The excerpt states that the Gateway API is designed with role-based personas in mind, in contrast to the Ingress model, which assumes a single persona where developers manage and create ingress and service resources themselves. In more complex deployments, infrastructure providers, cluster operators and application developers are all involved, and by deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require. The excerpt gives exactly this example: application developers in a specific team could be assigned permissions to create Route objects in a specified namespace without also gaining permissions to modify the Gateway configuration or edit Route objects in namespaces other than theirs.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite about annotations: native support of policies for external traffic means annotations are no longer required to support ingress traffic patterns. It never describes annotations as an ownership or access-control mechanism.
optionRationale.c: API conformance is mentioned only in connection with promoting common denominators as extensions are added, to maximise the ease of extending Ingress API resources. It is not described as granting namespace owners write access to the Gateway configuration.
optionRationale.d: The centralized mechanism for HTTP routing, TLS termination, traffic splitting/weighting and header modification is a genuine feature in the excerpt, but it is not offered as the reason why per-persona permissions can be scoped; the role-based persona design is.

citations.title: Benefits of the Gateway API
citations.quote: By deconstructing the Ingress API into several Gateway API objects, personas gain the specific access and privileges that their responsibilities require.

stem: An engineer creates an Ingress with an Exact path /api, an ImplementationSpecific path /api.*, a Prefix path /api, and a Prefix path /. A request for /api arrives. In the Envoy configuration that Cilium generates, which path's match is ordered first?

options.text: The Exact path /api
The ImplementationSpecific path /api.*
The Prefix path /api
The Prefix path /

explanation: Cilium orders Envoy matches by path type: Exact first, then ImplementationSpecific (regular expression), then Prefix, with the / Prefix match always last. The Exact /api match therefore precedes the ImplementationSpecific /api.* and the Prefix /api matches.

optionRationale.b: ImplementationSpecific matches are ordered after Exact matches, so /api.* is not first even though it is a regex path.
optionRationale.c: Prefix matches are ordered after both Exact and ImplementationSpecific matches.
optionRationale.d: The / Prefix match has special handling and always goes last, not first.

stem: An engineer runs Cilium 1.16 with the Gateway API enabled and switches on host network mode, because no LoadBalancer Service is available in the development cluster. One Gateway listener is configured on port 8080 and a TCPRoute is attached to that Gateway. What should the engineer expect to happen to the TCPRoute traffic?

options.text: It bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly, which is now a NodePort Service using a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than port 8080.
It is proxied through Envoy and served on port 8080 on all host interfaces, exactly as configured on the listener.
Host network mode is refused and the Gateway remains in LoadBalancer Service mode until the TCPRoute is removed.
It is served on port 8080, but only on the loopback interface, because host network mode binds listeners to 0.0.0.0.

explanation: Host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute. Their traffic bypasses Envoy and reaches the Gateway's generated Service directly. That Service would normally expose the configured Gateway listener port as a LoadBalancer Service, but enabling host network mode turns it into a NodePort Service, which receives a randomly assigned port from the node port range instead of the port configured on the listener. The engineer should therefore not assume that port 8080 is the port actually serving the TCPRoute traffic.

optionRationale.b: This describes the normal Envoy-proxied path on the configured listener port, but TCPRoute and UDPRoute traffic bypasses Envoy under host network mode and the generated Service becomes a NodePort Service with a random port.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states that host network mode is not compatible with TCPRoute and UDPRoute, not that enabling it is refused; the mode is enabled and the Service type changes instead.
optionRationale.d: The listener is exposed on all interfaces (0.0.0.0 for IPv4 and/or :: for IPv6), not on the loopback interface, and the port is not the configured listener port for these route types.

citations.title: Host network mode
citations.quote: Enabling host network mode turns this Service into a ``NodePort`` Service instead, which gets a randomly assigned port from the node port range rather than the port configured on the ``Gateway`` listener.

stem: You apply a `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` that denies all traffic by default, then run `curl --fail -v http://"$HTTP_INGRESS"/details/1` against the Cilium Ingress. According to the excerpt, what happens?

options.text: The request is denied: curl reports HTTP 403 Forbidden, and the Hubble flow shows the HTTP request DROPPED with a 403 response FORWARDED.
The request succeeds with HTTP 200 OK because the default-deny policy applies only to in-cluster traffic, not to external traffic arriving through the Ingress.
The request is denied with HTTP 503 Service Unavailable because Envoy cannot reach any backend once the policy is applied.
The request is dropped at the TCP layer, so curl reports a connection timeout rather than an HTTP status code.

explanation: With the default-deny `CiliumClusterwideNetworkPolicy` applied, the excerpt states that the request to the `/details` endpoint is denied for external and in-cluster traffic. The curl output shows `HTTP/1.1 403 Forbidden` with `server: envoy`, and the Hubble observe output shows the `http-request DROPPED` followed by an `http-response FORWARDED` carrying the 403.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the request is denied for external and in-cluster traffic, so external traffic through the Ingress is not exempt.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt shows a 403 Forbidden response, not a 503 Service Unavailable.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt shows an HTTP 403 response being returned, not a TCP-level connection timeout.

citations.quote: With this policy applied, the request to the ``/details`` endpoint will be denied for external and in-cluster traffic.

stem: A platform team has installed the standard release channel CRDs for Cilium Gateway API and now wants to use HTTPRoute Retry, which the excerpt identifies as an experimental feature in the HTTPRoute resource. What must the team do?

options.text: Install the corresponding CRDs; the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard channel plus experimental resources and fields.
Nothing further: the standard release channel already includes all experimental resources and fields.
Install the optional TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet CRDs, because those optional CRDs enable experimental HTTPRoute fields.
Only enable the Cilium Gateway API controller with Helm or Cilium CLI; the choice of CRD release channel has no bearing on experimental features.

explanation: The excerpt states that the experimental release channel includes everything in the standard release channel plus some experimental resources and fields. It gives HTTPRoute Retry in the HTTPRoute resource as an example of an experimental feature and states that, if you need such a feature, you must install the corresponding CRDs. The team therefore needs the corresponding CRDs, not merely the standard channel.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt lists TCPRoute, UDPRoute and ListenerSet as optional CRDs for their own functionality; it does not say they enable HTTPRoute Retry.

stem: A team exposes a service through Cilium Ingress. A request from outside the cluster reaches the per-node Envoy and is then sent to a backend Pod with the `productpage` identity. The team is writing Network Policy and wants the request to pass both logical policy enforcement points. Which pair of allowances must the policy provide?

options.text: Allow traffic from `world` to `ingress`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.
Allow traffic from `world` directly to `productpage`, and allow traffic from `ingress` to `world`.
Allow traffic only from `world` to `ingress`; the second enforcement point does not need a policy allowance.
Allow traffic only from `ingress` to `productpage`; external traffic is always assigned the `productpage` identity.

explanation: Cilium Ingress has two logical policy enforcement points: one before traffic arrives at the `ingress` identity and one after, when it is about to exit the per-node Envoy. The policy must therefore allow traffic from `world` to `ingress` and from `ingress` to in-cluster identities such as `productpage`.

optionRationale.b: This reverses the required direction and skips the `ingress` identity; the excerpt requires `world` to `ingress` and `ingress` to in-cluster identities.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says there are two logical enforcement points, so allowing only the first step is insufficient.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says traffic from outside the cluster is usually assigned the `world` identity, not `productpage`; the second step alone is insufficient.

This means that, when applying Network Policy to a cluster, it's important to
ensure that both steps are allowed, and that traffic is allowed from ``world`` to
``ingress``, and from ``ingress`` to identities in the cluster

stem: You have deployed the `pod-worker` client and the `echo` server, confirmed that `pod-worker` receives HTTP `200` from `http://echo:3000/headers` while `http://echo:3000/headers-1` is denied, and verified that the SPIRE server is healthy. According to the excerpt, what must you add to enforce mutual authentication between `pod-worker` and `echo`?

Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `echo` Service definition.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
Add `authentication.mode: "required"` to the SPIRE server configuration.

It does not say to modify the Service, the Pod manifest, or the SPIRE server configuration.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `echo` Service definition.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt places the setting in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the `pod-worker` Pod manifest.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says to verify that the SPIRE server is healthy, but it places `authentication.mode: "required"` in the ingress/egress block in your network policies, not in the SPIRE server configuration.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium Gateway API behind a trusted cloud load balancer. The load balancer injects an `X-Forwarded-For` header containing the original client IP. The team wants Cilium's Layer 7 policies, including Ingress, to be applied using that client IP rather than the address of the load balancer connection. Which configuration change matches the Cilium documentation?

options.text: Set `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` section of the values files.
Set the trusted hop count to `1` so Envoy uses the rightmost `X-Forwarded-For` value for policy decisions.
Set `useRemoteAddress` to `true` so Envoy trusts the `X-Forwarded-For` header.
Do nothing, because Envoy already uses `X-Envoy-External-Address` as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

explanation: The excerpt says that when you trust the traffic source to inject an `X-Forwarded-For` header, you can force Envoy to treat the traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in that header by setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false` in the `gatewayAPI` or `ingressController` sections of values files. The trusted-hop count changes how Envoy derives the visible source address for `X-Forwarded-For`, and `X-Envoy-External-Address` is a header Envoy sets; neither is the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the `X-Forwarded-For` client IP.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt describes the trusted-hop count as controlling which `X-Forwarded-For` value Envoy uses for the visible source address, not as the documented switch for making Layer 7 policy use the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt specifies setting `useRemoteAddress` to `false`, not `true`, to force Envoy to treat traffic as coming from the client IP encoded in `X-Forwarded-For`.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Envoy sets `X-Envoy-External-Address` to the trusted client address, but it does not say that this header is already used as the source for Layer 7 policy decisions.

citations.title: Source IP Visibility
citations.quote: ``useRemoteAddress`` to ``false`` in ``gatewayAPI`` or ``ingressController`` sections of values files.

stem: A Cilium cluster has WireGuard transparent encryption enabled. Two pods that are both scheduled on the same node exchange traffic with each other, and an engineer watching the node's traffic expects to see that traffic protected by the WireGuard tunnel. What does Cilium actually do with these packets?

options.text: It leaves them unencrypted, because traffic destined to the same node it was sent from is deliberately not encrypted.
It encrypts them, because WireGuard is enabled cluster-wide for every Cilium-managed endpoint.
It encrypts them only when the two pods belong to different namespaces.
It drops them unless a CiliumNetworkPolicy explicitly allows pod-to-pod traffic on that node.

explanation: WireGuard encryption in Cilium covers traffic between Cilium-managed endpoints on different nodes. When the source and the destination are the same node, the packets are not encrypted, and the excerpt states that this behaviour is intended: the raw traffic can be observed on the node anyway, so encryption would provide no benefit.

optionRationale.b: Enabling WireGuard does not encrypt every packet; the same-node case is explicitly excluded from encryption.
optionRationale.c: Namespace membership plays no part in the decision — the criterion given is whether the traffic is destined to the node it was sent from.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says nothing about dropping same-node traffic; it says such packets are simply not encrypted.

citations.title: WireGuard Transparent Encryption
citations.quote:
Packets are not encrypted when they are destined to the same node from which
they were sent. This behavior is intended.

stem: An engineer needs to retrieve the WireGuard public key that a particular cluster node has generated and shared with the rest of the cluster, so that it can be inspected with kubectl. Where does Cilium publish that key?

options.text: In the `network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key` annotation on the Kubernetes `CiliumNode` custom resource object.
In a Kubernetes Secret in the `kube-system` namespace, referenced by the Cilium agent DaemonSet.
In the `cilium-config` ConfigMap, under a per-node key entry.
In the status field of a `CiliumNetworkPolicy` object scoped to the node.

explanation: Each node creates its own encryption key-pair automatically and distributes the public half through the `network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key` annotation in the Kubernetes `CiliumNode` custom resource object. Other nodes then use that public key to encrypt and decrypt traffic to and from the Cilium-managed endpoints on that node.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt names an annotation on a ``CiliumNode`` object, not a Secret.
optionRationale.c: No ConfigMap is mentioned as the distribution mechanism for node public keys.
optionRationale.d: ``CiliumNetworkPolicy`` is not the object that carries the public key; the key lives on the ``CiliumNode`` resource.

distributes its public key via the ``network.cilium.io/wg-pub-key`` annotation
in the Kubernetes ``CiliumNode`` custom resource object.

stem: A platform team runs Cilium with WireGuard enabled on nodes that sit behind firewalls, and the tunnels between nodes are failing to establish. The team must open a single port between all Cilium cluster nodes so that the WireGuard tunnel endpoints can reach each other. Which port and protocol should the firewall rules permit?

options.text: UDP port `51871`.
TCP port `51871`.
UDP port `8472`.
TCP port `4240`.

explanation: The WireGuard tunnel endpoint is exposed on UDP port `51871` on each node. In an environment that requires firewall rules to enable connectivity, all Cilium cluster nodes must be able to reach each other via that port.

optionRationale.b: The port number is right but the protocol is wrong — the tunnel endpoint is exposed on UDP, not TCP.
optionRationale.c: ``8472`` is not the port given for the WireGuard tunnel endpoint in the excerpt.
optionRationale.d: ``4240`` is not the port given for the WireGuard tunnel endpoint in the excerpt.

stem: A cluster is configured to use tunnel routing mode and also has WireGuard encryption enabled. An engineer is analysing a pod-to-pod packet captured on the wire between two nodes and wants to know how many layers of encapsulation to expect and in which order they are applied. What should the engineer expect?

options.text: Two encapsulations: the packet is first sent to the VXLAN / Geneve tunnel interface and is then also encapsulated by the WireGuard tunnel.
Two encapsulations: the packet is first encapsulated by the WireGuard tunnel and is then sent to the VXLAN / Geneve tunnel interface.
One encapsulation: WireGuard encryption replaces the VXLAN / Geneve encapsulation entirely.
One encapsulation: only the VXLAN / Geneve tunnel is used, and WireGuard encrypts the payload without adding any encapsulation.

explanation: In tunnel routing mode, pod-to-pod traffic is encapsulated twice. It is first sent to the VXLAN / Geneve tunnel interface and is then subsequently also encapsulated by the WireGuard tunnel, so the WireGuard encapsulation is the outer of the two.

optionRationale.c: WireGuard does not replace the VXLAN / Geneve encapsulation in tunnel routing mode; both are applied.

stem: An engineer defines a Cilium Layer 7 HTTP policy rule that sets a Path regex but leaves the Method field empty. A client sends a POST request whose path matches the regex. What is the result?

options.text: The request is allowed, because an omitted or empty Method permits all methods.
The request is denied, because a Method must be specified explicitly for an HTTP rule to match.
The request is allowed only if it is a GET request, because GET is the default method.
The request is evaluated by matching the POST method against the Path regex.

explanation: The excerpt states that if Method is omitted or empty, all methods are allowed. The POST request is therefore permitted when its path matches the Path regex, and no separate Method value is required.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt does not require Method to be set; an omitted or empty Method allows all methods rather than causing a denial.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says all methods are allowed when Method is omitted or empty, not that GET becomes the only permitted method.
optionRationale.d: Method is matched against the method of a request, while Path is matched against the path of a request; the two fields are not interchangeable.

stem: A platform team runs a Cilium cluster whose nodes are spread across several routing domains, and the routers in the underlying network have no knowledge of the cluster's PodCIDRs. According to the excerpt, what does the encapsulation model require of that underlying network?

options.text: The underlying network must be configured with the PodCIDRs so that its routers can forward pod traffic.
The topology of the underlying network is irrelevant, provided the cluster nodes can reach each other using IP/UDP.
All cluster nodes must sit within a single link-layer domain for encapsulated traffic to flow.
The PodCIDR size must be chosen to fit within the addressing limitations of the underlying network.

explanation: The excerpt lists simplicity as an advantage of the model: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs, and cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains. The only requirement stated is reachability between nodes using IP/UDP, which makes the underlying topology irrelevant. Options a, c and d each contradict a specific statement in the excerpt.

optionRationale.a: The excerpt states the opposite: the network connecting the cluster nodes does not need to be made aware of the PodCIDRs.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says cluster nodes can spawn multiple routing or link-layer domains, so a single link-layer domain is not required.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says the addressing space does not depend on any underlying networking limitations, so the PodCIDR need not be fitted to them.

stem: In Cilium's encapsulation model, what purpose does the excerpt give for carrying the source security identity as metadata in the network packet?

options.text: It encrypts the packet payload between the cluster nodes.
It is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node.
It lets the remote node learn the PodCIDR of the sending node.
It removes the need for cluster nodes to reach each other using IP/UDP.

It then states that this identity transfer is an optimisation designed to avoid one identity lookup on the remote node. The other options describe functions the excerpt does not attribute to the identity transfer.

optionRationale.c: The excerpt does not link the identity transfer to PodCIDR discovery; it concerns the source security identity.

stem: An operator holds CAP_SYS_ADMIN in their own current user namespace and uses pod exec to enter a running Cilium agent container. Under what condition does this amount to privileged access?

options.text: Only if CAP_SYS_ADMIN is also held in the Cilium user namespace, which is the initial namespace.
Only if the operator also holds CAP_NET_ADMIN inside the Cilium container.
Always, because the Linux kernel permits joining other namespaces by default.
Only if the Cilium agent's volumes were mounted with unsafe options.

explanation: The kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, so entering the Cilium container requires CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both the current user namespace and the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace). When both namespaces carry that capability, the access is already privileged. Holding CAP_NET_ADMIN, kernel defaults or volume mount options play no part in this test.

optionRationale.b: CAP_NET_ADMIN is not the capability named in the excerpt; the test is CAP_SYS_ADMIN in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states the opposite: the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so mount options are not the deciding factor.

citations.quote: To enter the Cilium container, the ``CAP_SYS_ADMIN`` capability is required in both the current user namespace and in the Cilium user namespace (the initial namespace).

stem: A platform team discovers that developers can freely exec into Cilium pods in a shared cluster. Which two things does the excerpt say must be restricted to prevent privileged access to Cilium pods?

options.text: Access to the Kubernetes API and arbitrary pod exec operations.
Access to the /proc filesystem and the agent's Linux capabilities.
Volume mounts on the host and hostPath volume usage.
User namespace creation and the agent's CAP_SYS_ADMIN capability.

explanation: The excerpt's closing recommendation is to restrict access to the Kubernetes API and arbitrary pod exec operations. That follows from the earlier point that unrestricted pod exec lets a remote user exec into pods and containers, defeating Linux namespace restrictions. The other options name mechanisms the excerpt never presents as the controls to apply.

optionRationale.b: The /proc filesystem is described as a reason Cilium needs kernel interfaces, not as something to restrict.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt states Cilium performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount, so volume mounts are not the control named.
optionRationale.d: CAP_SYS_ADMIN is the capability required to enter the container; the excerpt does not recommend removing it from the agent.

stem: Why does the Cilium agent need kernel interfaces that cannot be virtualized or namespaced?

options.text: Because some kernel interfaces are part of the /proc filesystem, which includes host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.
Because Cilium mounts host volumes with unsafe options that bypass namespaces.
Because the Cilium agent runs without any Linux capabilities at all.
Because Kubernetes does not support user namespaces on cluster nodes.

explanation: The excerpt explains that Cilium needs kernel interfaces to configure the environment properly, and that some of these interfaces sit in the /proc filesystem, which carries host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced. The remaining options contradict the excerpt, which says Cilium needs specific Linux capabilities and performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt explicitly says Cilium doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt opens by stating the Cilium agent needs some specific Linux capabilities.
optionRationale.d: User namespace support is not discussed; the limitation given is about /proc contents, not Kubernetes support.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: Some kernel interfaces are part of the ``/proc`` filesystem, which includes host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.

stem: A security reviewer asks whether the Cilium agent itself performs extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount. How does the excerpt answer?

options.text: No: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes, and performs no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
Yes: the agent mounts /proc directly using privileged mount options.
Yes: the agent needs CAP_SYS_ADMIN specifically in order to mount host volumes.
No: the agent mounts no volumes at all in a Cilium deployment.

explanation: The excerpt contrasts Cilium's behaviour with what a reviewer might fear: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes, and it doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount. Saying it mounts nothing at all is also wrong, since the excerpt refers to mounting the corresponding volumes.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the opposite: no extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.
optionRationale.c: CAP_SYS_ADMIN appears in the excerpt as the capability needed to enter the Cilium container, not as a mount requirement.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt states that Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to mount the corresponding volumes, so it is not true that no volumes are mounted.

citations.title: Background
citations.quote: Cilium relies on Kubernetes and containers to set up the environment and mount the corresponding volumes. Cilium doesn't perform any extra operations that could result in an unsafe volume mount.

stem: An auditor finds that a user who is not a cluster administrator can exec into a Cilium pod and reach beyond the container's namespace boundaries. According to the excerpt, what is the root cause of this exposure?

options.text: Pod exec operations are not restricted, so remote exec into pods and containers defeats Linux namespace restrictions.
The Linux kernel allows joining other namespaces by default, so no capability is ever needed.
The Cilium agent runs in the initial user namespace without any capabilities.
The /proc filesystem is virtualized per container, so exec bypasses it.

explanation: The excerpt states that if pod exec operations aren't restricted, then remote exec into pods and containers defeats Linux namespace restrictions. The kernel does not permit namespace joining by default, and the agent does need specific Linux capabilities, so the other explanations invert the excerpt's facts.

optionRationale.b: The excerpt says the Linux kernel restricts joining other namespaces by default, and that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is required in both namespaces.
optionRationale.c: The excerpt says the Cilium agent needs some specific Linux capabilities, and that CAP_SYS_ADMIN is required in the Cilium user namespace.
optionRationale.d: The excerpt says some kernel interfaces in /proc include host and machine configurations that can't be virtualized or namespaced.
